title: Postmortems & Incident Learning
summary: An incident that's resolved but not learned from will happen again. Learn how blameless postmortems, the 5 whys, and tracked action items turn a single outage into durable organizational defense.

slides.markdown:
[on-call-and-incident-response](on-call-and-incident-response) ends at **resolve** — impact has stopped. But the incident isn't actually over until **follow-up** happens, and skipping it is how the same class of failure quietly recurs six months later, sometimes to a different team who never heard about the first one.

A **postmortem** is how an organization converts one team's hard-won, 2am understanding of a failure into something everyone can learn from without living through it themselves. Done well, it's the highest-leverage document engineering teams write — a few hours of structured reflection buying protection against a repeat that could cost days.

Done badly — vague, blame-focused, no real action items — it's a box-checking exercise nobody reads twice, and the org pays for the same outage again.

slides.subTitle: Why blame suppresses the honest detail you need
slides.markdown:
**Blameless** doesn't mean "nobody made a mistake" — it means the postmortem's questions target the **system**, not the **person**: not "who deployed the bad config" but "why did our tooling let a bad config reach production without being caught, and why didn't we catch it faster."

The reason this matters practically, not just culturally: if engineers expect blame, they give vague or defensive answers, or quietly leave out the detail that actually explains the failure ("I was tired and missed the review comment" becomes "the review process could be clearer"). That missing detail is exactly the input a good fix needs. A blameless process gets the honest version because there's no cost to giving it.

Blameless also isn't a synonym for "no accountability" — action items still get owners and due dates. The distinction is that the *process of investigation* doesn't punish honesty, while the *outcome* still holds the org accountable for fixing what's broken.

slides.subTitle: Timeline, impact, root cause(s), action items
slides.markdown:
A useful postmortem has a consistent shape, so anyone in the org can skim any postmortem and find what they need:

- **Timeline** — what happened, in order, with real timestamps: when the change shipped, when the alert fired, when someone acknowledged, when it was mitigated, when it fully resolved.
- **Impact** — concretely quantified: how many users, how long, what specifically broke (failed checkouts, elevated latency, data inconsistency) — not just "the service was down."
- **Root cause(s)** — the mechanism, ideally more than the first proximate trigger (see the 5 whys next).
- **Action items** — specific, owned, dated tasks that would have prevented this or caught it faster, not vague intentions.

The timeline in particular does double duty: it's the raw material for computing time-to-detect and time-to-mitigate, which matter as much as the root cause for judging how well the *response* worked, independent of how the bug itself happened.

slides.subTitle: Digging past the first proximate cause
slides.markdown:
The **5 whys** technique: state the failure, ask "why did that happen," and for each answer, ask "why" again — typically five iterations reaches something a fix can actually address, versus stopping at the first, most obvious layer.

```
1. Why did checkout fail?          → the payment service crashed
2. Why did it crash?               → it ran out of memory
3. Why did it run out of memory?   → a cache grew unbounded
4. Why did the cache grow unbounded? → no eviction policy was configured
5. Why was there no eviction policy? → the cache library defaults to unbounded, and nothing in review or CI checks for it
```

Stopping at why #1 or #2 ("the service crashed, restart it and move on" or "add more memory") fixes the symptom for this exact instance. Reaching why #5 finds something fixable at the *systemic* level — a CI check or a linting rule that catches unbounded caches in review — which prevents the entire class of bug, not just this one occurrence of it.

slides.subTitle: Incidents are rarely one cause
slides.markdown:
Real incidents are usually a **stack of contributing factors** that all had to line up, not one single root cause — which is why the postmortem template says "root cause(s)," plural. A bad config was the trigger, but it also had to pass review unnoticed, deploy without a canary catching it, and reach a system with no circuit breaker to contain the blast radius. Remove any one of those four and the incident either doesn't happen or is far smaller.

Treating it as one root cause tends to fixate on the most visible factor (usually the trigger — the bad config, the specific commit) and miss the others, which are just as fixable and often more valuable: a canary that would have caught this bad config would also catch the next one, regardless of what it is.

A useful postmortem lists every contributing factor it can find and proposes an action item for more than one of them, not just the trigger.

| | Single-root-cause narrative | Systems view |
|---|---|---|
| Framing | "An engineer pushed a bad config" | "A bad config passed review, deployment, and canary checks without being caught" |
| Action items produced | Usually one — fix that config, remind engineers to be careful | Several — canary coverage, review checklist, circuit breaker, alerting threshold |
| Repeat protection | Low — the next bad *anything* still gets through the same gaps | High — the gaps that let this through are closed regardless of what triggers the next incident |
| Morale effect | Implicitly blames the individual who happened to trigger it | Treats the trigger as inevitable eventually, and asks why the system didn't catch it |

The systems view isn't just kinder — it's more effective, because "be more careful" doesn't scale as a fix and doesn't survive the next engineer who makes an equally human mistake. Closing the systemic gaps protects against triggers nobody has thought of yet.

slides.sectionTitle: Action items with owners and due dates
slides.markdown:
A postmortem's real value is entirely in whether its action items get done — brilliant root-cause analysis with no follow-through prevents nothing. Two properties separate an action item that gets done from one that quietly dies:

- **A named owner**, not a team or "we should." "The observability team will add a canary check" gets done; "we should improve canary coverage" is everyone's job and therefore no one's.
- **A due date**, tracked in the same system as regular work (a ticket in the normal backlog, not a line in a document nobody revisits) — so it competes for prioritization visibly instead of silently losing to whatever's more urgent this sprint.

A good practice: a lightweight recurring review (monthly, or at a regular engineering sync) of open postmortem action items specifically, separate from the general backlog review, so "this incident's fix" doesn't get permanently deprioritized in favor of new feature work.

slides.subTitle: Normalizing failure as a learning input
slides.markdown:
A postmortem kept private to the team that had the incident only protects that team. Sharing it broadly — a searchable internal archive, a recurring "incident review" discussion open to the org, a summary in a company-wide channel — turns one team's expensive lesson into a discount for every other team that might hit something similar.

This has a second-order cultural effect too: when postmortems are visible and clearly blameless in practice (not just in name), engineers see that reporting and analyzing failure honestly is rewarded, not punished — which makes the *next* postmortem more honest too. Teams that hide incidents, by contrast, signal that failure is shameful, which drives future incidents further underground and further from the systemic fixes they need.

The practical habit worth building: before starting a new project or design, a quick search of past postmortems for the area you're touching — someone likely already paid to learn a lesson relevant to what you're about to build.

slides.sectionTitle: Great analysis, action items that never get done
slides.markdown:
The most common way a postmortem fails despite looking excellent on paper: the timeline is precise, the 5 whys genuinely reach a systemic cause, the writing is thoughtful — and then the action items sit in a document, unowned or under-prioritized, and six months later the same class of incident recurs because nothing actually changed.

This happens because writing the analysis feels like the finish line — it's satisfying, it's the intellectually interesting part, and once it's published there's a natural sense of closure. But the analysis prevented nothing on its own; only the action items do, and they compete with every other piece of planned work for the same limited engineering time, usually without an equivalent champion pushing for them.

The structural fix: track postmortem action items as first-class tickets in the normal work-tracking system, assign a real owner and due date at postmortem time (not "later"), and review open items on a fixed cadence — treating an unresolved high-value action item as itself a signal worth escalating, the same way an open incident would be.

Putting it together: the timeline shows a config deployed at 2:03pm, an alert at 2:11pm, mitigation (rollback) at 2:19pm, fully resolved at 2:24pm — 21 minutes of impact affecting roughly 4% of checkout traffic. The 5 whys trace past "bad config" to "no CI check validates cache eviction settings." The write-up lists four contributing factors, not one: the config itself, a review that didn't catch it, no canary stage before full rollout, and no automated alert on the specific memory metric that would have caught it faster than the 8-minute detection time.

Four action items follow, each with an owner and a date: add the CI check (owner: platform team, two weeks), add a canary stage to this deploy pipeline (owner: the team, one sprint), add the missing memory alert (owner: SRE, one week), and update the review checklist (owner: tech lead, immediate). The document is shared in the org-wide incident channel. Three of the four items are done within the month, tracked as normal tickets — and the next engineer who almost makes the same config mistake gets caught by CI before it ever reaches production.

This closes the group's arc: [systematic-debugging-method](systematic-debugging-method) gave you the loop for one bug, [reading-stack-traces-and-logs](reading-stack-traces-and-logs) and [debugging-tools-techniques](debugging-tools-techniques) gave you the evidence and tools, [production-debugging-observability](production-debugging-observability) and [concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs](concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs) covered the hardest cases, and [on-call-and-incident-response](on-call-and-incident-response) covered the team response under pressure.

A postmortem is where all of that becomes an asset instead of a memory — the difference between a team that gets steadily better at not repeating its mistakes, and one that relearns the same lesson every year with a different name attached. The skill isn't just finding bugs; it's making sure each one only has to be found once.
